title: EC pledges to strengthen member states’ response to security threats
content:
Particular attention should be paid to plans for a new EU security strategy, including proposals for a Security Council and an EU alert mechanism to respond to security threats that do not reach the level of armed aggression. Critics have previously warned that such a move could risk overlapping with NATO security mechanisms.

With the war in Ukraine increasingly affecting Europe’s eastern flank and Russia stepping up its sabotage attacks and drone campaigns, security and defence became the main theme of the European Commission president’s annual address.

This week alone, Poland raised the alarm after Russia struck a train travelling from Kyiv to Warsaw. At the time of the attack, the train was at the Yahodyn railway station, approximately two kilometres from the Ukrainian-Polish border. Shortly afterwards, Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that such escalations were increasingly approaching the borders of European countries: “The coming weeks and months are expected to be a very intense period in Russia’s activities.”

title: Did the EU force Google to remove hotel prices from its search engine?
content:
On the 9th of September, an anonymous account on the social network X published a post about changes made by Google to its search engine in Europe. The post is partly true, but supplements the facts with unfounded conclusions about EU requirements and Google’s motives, implying that changes making the popular search engine less convenient for Europeans were introduced as a result of decisions made in Brussels.

On the 8th of September, Google did indeed introduce changes to search results in the European Union. They affect, for example, how search results for hotels, airlines, and restaurants are displayed. In some European countries, certain sections of the service no longer show features that were previously available, such as real-time prices. Most of the changes are linked to decisions adopted by the European Commission (EC) in July concerning Google’s compliance with the Digital Markets Act.

The EC imposed two fines on Google totalling 890 million euros. A 460 million euros fine was imposed because Google gave preference in its search results to its own services, such as Google Flights and Google Hotels, over competing services.

title: Mustard Gas, Phosgene or Something Else? How the Czech Government’s Strategic Communication Failed
content:
MP Filip Turek first said mustard gas was leaking into the soil, then changed his claim to phosgene and later said the substances could turn into phosgene under certain conditions. A crisis communication expert told Update EU that the episode showed how the absence of a clear communication strategy can turn evolving information into public confusion.

Shortly after taking office, the Czech government abolished or reorganised crisis and strategic communication capacities within government institutions. In March, the Interior Ministry abolished its Crisis Information Team (KRIT), which had coordinated state communication with the public during crises such as floods and power outages. The ministry said the change would bring savings, 

The absence of crisis communication expertise became particularly evident in the case of hazardous substances leaking into the soil in Šumava National Park. In early September, Environment Minister Igor Červený announced that remediation work was beginning on barrels from a former military area in southern Czechia containing hazardous substances that were leaking into the soil.

title: Canada-EU alliance could be “beacon” for other democracies, Carney says. Australia is interested, Kyiv worries
content:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s State of the Union address stirred debate around the idea of a new form of closer association between Canada and the EU. Just a day later, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney also took the floor in parliament. 

He clearly welcomed the idea of his country becoming a closer partner of the Union. He noted that a large majority of Canadians also support closer ties with Brussels and outlined how he envisages the functioning of the “new alliance”.  

“We are not fair-weather allies. We do not pursue zero-sum deals. Our commitment to the rule of law and our unyielding defence of human dignity, individual freedom and democracy share the same deep roots,” he said during his Thursday speech in Strasbourg. 

Carney noted that the world is currently being shaken by new challenges, from climate shocks and the undermining of democratic institutions to the weaponisation of the economy and various unfair practices by technology platforms.

title: Is Latvia “one big training ground” where you cannot pick mushrooms?
content:
The National Armed Forces (NAF) Law defines a military training ground as a geographically designated area of the territorial sea or land territory of the Republic of Latvia, as well as the airspace above this territory, where military exercises, manoeuvres involving the use of training and combat ammunition, tactical training and host-nation support are carried out, the ministry explained.

There are five military training grounds in Latvia:

  • the Ādaži military training ground;
  • the Mežaine military training ground in Kurzeme;
  • the Lāčusils military training ground in Vidzeme;
  • the Meža Mackeviči military training ground in Latgale;
  • the Sēlija military training ground.

    • Latvia also has two military aviation training areas: in Ādaži and Jūrmalciems.

    According to the MoD, the total area of the military training grounds is approximately 43 000 hectares, of which the Sēlija military training ground occupies 24 500 hectares.

title: No further than the idea stage: defence start-ups struggle to secure start-up funding
content:
Once a company has demonstrated the potential of its technology and development begins to accelerate, securing funding becomes relatively easy. Getting to this point is much harder, meaning that many start-ups never get beyond the idea stage because they lack funding.

For defence-sector companies to develop rapidly, money is needed not only when they have already achieved their first successes, but also at the very beginning – to develop the idea, build a prototype and test the technology. Yet, the funding currently available falls far short of covering all companies’ needs. This means that a promising idea may never progress beyond the initial stage – not because it lacks potential, but because the company does not have sufficient resources to demonstrate that potential.

title: How Poland “planned to occupy Czech lands” – coordinated information operation exposed
content:
Facebook posts called on people to gather for a protest in the Czech border town of Třinec on Saturday, 29th of August. The protest never took place. The Třinec municipal authorities had already announced that no public event had been registered, while the Czech Republic’s largest trade union, KOVO, which represents metalworking and industrial workers and whose logo was used in the protest advertising materials, denied any connection with the action. Moreover, Polish and Czech media had already exposed the disinformation campaign, which involved fake social media profiles, fabricated media outlets, forged documents and even an unauthorised publication of an article on the website of a public broadcaster.

At the beginning of August, disinformation began circulating claiming that Poland planned to take over more than 600 hectares of Czech territory. According to an analysis by the Czech news portal Seznam Zprávy, several social media accounts in the Czech Republic circulated a document purportedly sent by the Polish government to the Czech authorities. It allegedly demanded that land with a total area of 638.44 hectares be handed over to Poland.

title: Europe heard Draghi. Now it has to act
content:
The report by Mario Draghi, The Future of European Competitiveness, published on 9 September 2024, was intended as a response to the widening gap between the European economy and its US and Chinese competitors.

The former president of the European Central Bank pointed to low productivity, insufficient investment in new technologies, high energy prices, fragmentation of the single market and difficulties in financing European companies.

Draghi called for a deeper single market, simpler regulation, better access to finance and the mobilisation of additional public and private investment. He estimated that the EU needed around €750–800 billion in additional investment every year — equivalent to 4.4–4.7% of EU GDP — to finance the transition and restore economic dynamism.

Two years later, the core of Draghi’s diagnosis has been broadly accepted in Brussels. The implementation of his prescriptions, however, tells a much less impressive story.

title: ‘Kyiv regime and EU patrons are looting Crimean treasures’: Russian exhibition in Bratislava pushes Kremlin propaganda
content:
The Russian Embassy in Slovakia this week announced on social media the opening of a photo exhibition in Bratislava titled “Crimean Gold: ‘Civilised’ Europe Plunders Russian Treasures”. 

The exhibition, organised by the Russian Military Historical Society, presents annexed Ukrainian Crimea as Russian territory and offers its version of the dispute with the Netherlands over archaeological artefacts from Crimean museums. 

The artefacts were temporarily displayed in Amsterdam. Following Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014, Dutch courts ruled that they should not be returned to the occupied peninsula but directly to Ukraine, which has a legitimate right to protect its cultural heritage. 

In a Facebook post, the Russian Embassy openly challenges that decision. It calls it a “dangerous precedent of politicising cultural heritage” and claims that the exhibits were stolen by the “Kyiv regime together with its European patrons”. 

EuBrief contacted the Foreign Ministry and the City of Bratislava about the exhibition on Friday.

title: Europe’s Housing Crisis: Why Young People Can’t Afford to Move Out
content:
Public debate often returns to a damaging stereotype: that today’s young people are a generation without ambition — lazy, overly comfortable and reluctant to leave the safety of the family home.

Yet the reality revealed by Eurostat’s latest data for 2024 paints a very different and far more complex picture. Young adults in the countries of Europe’s eastern flank are not living with their parents because they want to. They simply have to. Their first steps into adulthood amount to a collision with a housing market in which even the smallest — and often questionable-quality — apartments have become a luxury reserved for the few.

Eurostat data clearly show that the average age at which young Europeans leave the parental home now stands at 26.2. But that is only an average, masking enormous differences across the continent, particularly along its eastern flank.

The exception — one the rest of the region can only look at with envy — is Finland. Young people there leave home earlier than anywhere else in the European Union, at an average age of just 21.4.
